topics.title: Twine: Buy and Sell CKB Without Depositing on an Exchange (Fiber P2P PoC)

recent_posts.topic_title: Twine: Buy and Sell CKB Without Depositing on an Exchange (Fiber P2P PoC)
recent_posts.author: quake
recent_posts.content_text:
I think this is a good idea, and the PoC is well done. The UI already makes the basic trading and dispute resolution flows clear
For the next step, I suggest adding more on defining clear rules: how evidence is verified, who can take which actions, and who is responsible when something goes wrong. Tests showing that these rules hold up when payments fail, time out, or are disputed would go a long way toward building trust.

recent_posts.topic_title: Twine: Buy and Sell CKB Without Depositing on an Exchange (Fiber P2P PoC)
recent_posts.author: ebubedev
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks Quake.
I took that approach: the rules are written down, and the daemon tests fail if a payment, a timeout, or a dispute breaks them.
Fiat stays off the protocol. A receipt is a JPEG or PNG the buyer uploaded. The solver reads that picture, the chat, and the order. Nothing checks a bank. What the tests lock down is the daemon’s order state machine: which Fiber RPCs it calls, and which calls it refuses, against a mock Fiber node. They do not run CKB or a real fnn. The hold is a Fiber invoice. This code never force-closes a channel.
Who can act
Seller: accept the hold, release (including during an open dispute, if the buyer already sent a payout invoice), file a dispute, or agree to walk away.
Buyer: mark paid and upload the receipt, file a dispute, agree to walk away, or retry after a failed payout.
Solver: take the case with TWINE_SOLVER_TOKEN, then pay the buyer or refund the seller. Take and both award routes reject any other token. An award before take is rejected. The order room cannot award.
Daemon: if the trade is FiatSent and the invoice is still Received, it opens a dispute two hours before hold_by, with dispute_from = twine, and leaves S on the watchtower. That gives a solver time to call settle_invoice before Fiber expires. It does not stop the timelock. If nobody settles, the hold still expires. A hold whose pay window closed, and where fiat was never marked sent, is left for Fiber to expire.
Filing a dispute does not freeze Fiber’s clock, and it does not freeze the two parties. Until the solver awards, the seller can still release, or both sides can agree to walk away. It takes both. After an award or a walk-away, those actions stop.
When something goes wrong
If the payout to the buyer cannot route, settle_invoice is not called. The hold stays Received and the state is Leg2Failed. The buyer retries with a new invoice.
A Received hold is refunded by Fiber’s timelock. cancel_invoice is not called on it. An Open hold can still be cancelled inside the 15-minute accept window.
S is stored in the daemon and registered on the Twine node with create_preimage. GET /trades never returns it. The watchtower copy stays through FiatSent, Leg2Failed, and a dispute opened from those states, so a force-close can still be claimed while the trade can still settle. remove_preimage drops that copy on cancel, when the pay window closes, when the solver refunds the seller, on a mutual walk-away, after a successful settle, and when the timelock expires. The daemon’s own copy stays in market.json.
Tests (daemon/src/order/poc_test.rs)
cargo test in daemon/ runs these against the mock Fiber node:
failed_payment_does_not_settle_until_retry_pays
received_hold_timeout_refunds_seller_and_settle_fails
dispute_freezes_release_and_award_follows_the_hold
parties_can_release_or_abandon_an_open_dispute
fiat_sent_near_hold_expiry_opens_a_dispute_without_dropping_the_preimage
built_in_watchtower_holds_the_preimage_until_the_trade_ends
The same rules are in the README under “Four endings” and “Disputes”. The open gap is the one you pointed at: the solver is still trusting a picture. Nothing in this PoC proves the fiat moved.

topics.title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Where this thread has led me: trust before money
Thanks to everyone who contributed. A few points changed my thinking:
@janx: node operators already get non-monetary returns (trustlessness, privacy), and service income only helps CKB if it actually brings more full nodes.
@joshyates1980: many of us run nodes simply to support Nervos, and some recognition would already mean a lot.
@LusoCryptoLabs: light-client serving is a service only a real full node can provide, and it has to stay free.
So my conclusion: any service layer must stay outside the node, as a separate, optional tool, never part of ckb itself. And trust has to come before money.
What I’m sketching now, working title CKB Node Runner:
A dashboard for node runners. Node health, sync, peers and alerts, plus a live view that makes CKB’s cell model visible (cells consumed → cells created). Useful on its own, no payments involved.
An optional, public node ranking. Availability, sync lag, version, age and network diversity, keyed by node ID (never IP), with a verifiable summary published on-chain. It rewards long-term reliable operators with reputation, the “signature of acknowledgment” idea in a first form.
Only after ~12 months of ranking data: an optional service runtime, where ranked full nodes can take paid jobs. By then there’s a track record to choose nodes from, and time for applications to be built on it.
Would you install such a dashboard on your node? And what would you want it to show?

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks for pulling this together. A few things that may help.
Your first step is the same one Jan proposed as CKB Node Ninjas in the related thread post #2, a daemon beside the node and an ethstats-style site, funded by the Community DAO, which would pick rewards among the reporting nodes. That may be a path to funding the dashboard. His sybil point carries over too, node IDs are free to create, so availability and age would do most of the work.
“Network diversity” and “never IP” pull against each other. Publishing each node’s network operator (ASN) and region, without the address, keeps both. ckbadger’s crawler already records discovery, sessions and dial results, and its README says what that does not prove.
What we would want it to show: which nodes serve light clients (LightClient and Filter in their protocols), and which offer a public RPC. In the related thread, phroi counted two public RPC nodes he could query from a web app.
On proving a service runs on a full node: our resolver can read from any public node, and that is fine, because every answer carries a proof a client can check. Where an answer can be checked, where it runs stops mattering.

On proofs: agreed, a proven answer doesn’t depend on which node served it. I’d still require a full node, to reward nodes that make the network stronger and enhance trust: each paid service should come with another running full node.

topics.title: FiberNuts Community Market: A Testnet App for Cashu + Fiber

recent_posts.topic_title: FiberNuts Community Market: A Testnet App for Cashu + Fiber
recent_posts.author: Code3ks
recent_posts.content_text:
Gm CKB community,
In my earlier FiberNuts post, I said the next step should be more than improving the wallet. It should be a high-level application that shows why Cashu + Fiber could be useful in an everyday setting.
That application is now built: FiberNuts Community Market.
The idea is a small community event where attendees can buy items or tip contributors with RUSD ecash, while vendors receive and secure those payments before cashing out through Fiber.
Fiber moves RUSD into and out of the system. Cashu handles the many lightweight payments in between.
What the demo looks like
The application has two separate experiences:
Attendee: market.fibernuts.xyz
Vendor terminal: market.fibernuts.xyz/vendor
A complete payment works like this:
The attendee adds RUSD ecash by paying a Fiber invoice.
The vendor selects an item, such as a 2.50 RUSD coffee, and creates a payment request.
The attendee scans one QR code and reviews the amount, mint, fee, and remaining balance before paying.
The attendee wallet creates a Cashu payment locked to the vendor’s key and delivers it through the payment relay.
The vendor stores the received payment, checks it with the issuing mint, and swaps it for fresh proofs.
The order becomes Paid only after those fresh proofs are stored in the vendor balance.
The vendor can later cash out by asking the mint to pay an external RUSD Fiber invoice.
The distinction in step 6 is important. Delivered means the payment reached the vendor flow; it does not mean settlement is complete. The vendor sees Paid only after the issuing mint accepts the proofs and returns fresh ones.
What was added beyond the wallet
This is a focused event-payment application rather than another general wallet dashboard. It includes:
A vendor catalog, order builder, QR checkout, current order, and order history.
A one-scan NUT-18 payment flow with an exact review screen before value moves.
Vendor-key locking so the delivery relay cannot redeem the payment itself.
Separate attendee and vendor balances and operation histories.
Add-cash and cash-out flows that use Fiber at the boundaries.
Recovery states for interrupted delivery, settlement, issuance, and cash-out operations.
Persistent network, asset, mint, and testnet identification throughout the interface.
The trust boundary is still visible
This demo does not change the underlying Cashu trust model. The mint remains custodial and controls issuance, swaps, and redemption. Browser storage is not a secure backup, mint availability does not prove solvency, and a user still needs a funded RUSD Fiber route to add cash or cash out.
The current vendor-locked payment also has no attendee refund path after confirmation. That makes the relay unable to spend the payment, but it means this version should be used only with small testnet values while refund semantics are designed and tested properly.
The goal is not to hide these boundaries. It is to show a practical application while making the exact moment of settlement and the remaining custodial risk understandable.
What I would like feedback on
Does the attendee-and-vendor flow make the role of Cashu + Fiber clearer than the standalone wallet?
Would a community event or meetup be a useful place to test this with several attendees and vendors?
What information should a user see before accepting ecash from a mint?
What recovery or refund behavior would you require before using this beyond a controlled testnet demo?
The source is available at github.com/code3ks/fibernuts. The application, mint, and payment relay are deployed for use with CKB testnet, but please treat them as experimental infrastructure and use test value only.

topics.title: Spark Program | DAO Cycle Alerts: Telegram reminders before your Nervos DAO cycle ends

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | DAO Cycle Alerts: Telegram reminders before your Nervos DAO cycle ends
recent_posts.author: yukikawata
recent_posts.content_text:
English
1. Project overview
Name: DAO Cycle Alerts
One line: A read-only Telegram bot and CLI that tell Nervos DAO depositors when each deposit’s 180-epoch cycle is about to end, so they start a withdrawal in time and do not lose another 30 days.
Type: user tool (Telegram bot) plus developer tool (npm package and CLI).
2. Team profile
Yuki Kawata: sole developer and maintainer.
Past work: TheYukiKawata (Yuki Kawata) · GitHub (ton-checkout, arc-tabs, arc-till: payment tools on TON and Arc, deployed on Cloudflare Workers).
Contact: yuki@yukikawata.fyi (email only).
3. Project background
A Nervos DAO deposit unlocks only at the end of a 180-epoch cycle, about 30 days (RFC 23). You can start a withdrawal (phase 1) at any time, but the CKB stays locked until the current cycle ends. The deposit also stops earning compensation from that moment.
So the best time to start phase 1 is a few hours before the cycle ends. If you miss it by a day, the deposit rolls into a new cycle and you wait about 30 more days.
Today you find out where your deposit sits in its cycle only by opening Neuron or another wallet and checking. Nothing tells you ahead of time. There are 16,696 depositors holding 8.12 billion CKB in the DAO (CKB Explorer, 2026-09-26). Many of them hold long term and do not open a wallet every week.
Scenario: Li deposited 50,000 CKB in March and wants the CKB back for a purchase in October. She opens Neuron on October 3, starts the withdrawal, and learns that the cycle ended on October 1. The CKB unlocks on October 31.
4. Solution
In Telegram, the user sends /watch <ckb address>. The bot lists each DAO deposit with its cycle end time.
The bot sends a message 3 days and 12 hours before each cycle end: “Deposit of 50,000 CKB (tx 0xab..): cycle ends in about 12 hours (epoch 9123, around 2026-10-01 14:00 UTC). Start the withdrawal in your wallet before then to unlock at that time.”
For deposits already in phase 1, the bot sends a message when phase 2 becomes possible: “Your withdrawing deposit can be unlocked now.”
/list shows every watched deposit. /forget deletes the address and chat data.
The bot never asks for keys, signatures or wallet connections. It reads public chain data only.
Differences from existing tools: wallets show a countdown only while you have them open. This tool sends the reminder to you, and it works for any address, including cold wallets and multisig.
5. Technical approach
Language: TypeScript. Runtime: Cloudflare Workers with a cron trigger every 30 minutes. Storage: Cloudflare D1 (chat id, address, sent reminders).
Chain data: CKB public RPC and indexer (get_cells filtered by the Nervos DAO type script and the user’s lock script, get_header for deposit epochs, get_tip_header for the current epoch).
Core library dao-cycle (built, see section 9), on top of CCC:
find the address’s Nervos DAO cells and classify them as deposited (data is 8 zero bytes) or withdrawing (data is the deposit block number);
compute the unlock epoch with the DAO script’s own rule (c/dao.c): count the epochs from deposit to withdrawal, round up to a multiple of 180 (at least 180), add that to the deposit epoch. For a deposited cell the withdrawal epoch is the current tip, so the result is the end of the current cycle;
estimate wall-clock time from the average epoch length over the last 300,000 blocks (about 180 epochs).
CLI: dao-cycle check <address> prints the same table the bot uses.
Hardest part: accurate time estimates, since epoch length changes. The bot states times as “around” and re-checks every 30 minutes, so the 12-hour reminder uses fresh data.
Language: English, with Chinese message templates.
AI use: code, tests and docs are written with an AI coding agent (Claude).
Testing: the unlock epoch math is covered by tests, including RFC 23’s example transaction, and was checked against CCC’s calcDaoClaimEpoch on 150 mainnet withdrawing cells.
6. To-do list
Week 1: Telegram bot on Cloudflare Workers. /watch, /list, /forget, D1 storage, cron job. Milestone: bot answers /watch on mainnet.
Week 2: Reminders. 3-day and 12-hour messages, “ready to unlock” message, reminder de-duplication, Chinese and English messages, simulate command. Milestone: reminders live, dao-cycle published to npm.
Week 3: Seed users. Announce on Nervos Talk and CKB community channels. Target: 20 watched addresses. Collect feedback and fix issues.
Week 4: Completion report: usage numbers, reminders sent, feedback, fund usage.
7. Required funding and breakdown
Total: $1,000, paid in CKB.
Technical work (weeks 1 and 2): $700. Bot, reminders, simulate command, npm release, tests, deployment.
User testing (weeks 3 and 4): $200. Onboarding seed users, fixes from feedback, completion report.
Hosting: $100. Runs on the Cloudflare Workers free tier. This covers a paid tier or a dedicated RPC endpoint if load or rate limits require it, for 12 months after completion.
8. Deliverables and how to verify
Deliverables:
Public GitHub repository (MIT) with the library, CLI and bot.
npm package dao-cycle with the CLI.
Live Telegram bot on mainnet.
Completion report on Nervos Talk.
How to verify (no code review needed):
Unlock math: bun install && bun test. Expected: all tests pass, including the RFC 23 case (deposit at epoch 2+648/1677, withdrawing cell at 47+382/1605, unlock at 182+648/1677).
CLI against real data: bunx dao-cycle check <any address with a DAO deposit>. Expected: one row per deposit with the next cycle end epoch. Compare it with the same address in Neuron or CKB Explorer.
Bot: send /watch <address> to the bot. Expected: the same table within a minute.
Reminder timing without waiting 30 days: bunx dao-cycle simulate <address> --at-epoch <epoch> prints the reminders the bot would send at that epoch.
Privacy: /forget, then /list. Expected: “No addresses watched.”
Environment: Bun 1.x on any OS, internet access, a Telegram account. About 10 minutes in total.
9. Current state and funded work
Current state: the core library and CLI work on mainnet: GitHub - TheYukiKawata/dao-cycle: Find when each Nervos DAO deposit on a CKB address reaches the end of its 180-epoch cycle · GitHub (MIT). Run bun install && bun src/cli.ts check <address> to see each DAO cell on an address with its unlock epoch, estimated time and time left. Tests pass in CI, including the RFC 23 example. The unlock math gave the same result as CCC’s calcDaoClaimEpoch on the 150 newest withdrawing cells on mainnet.
Funded work: the Telegram bot, reminders, simulate command, npm release, seed users and the completion report (sections 6 and 8).
10. CKB alignment
The tool depends on CKB features: the Nervos DAO type script, cell data as the deposit/withdrawing marker, and absolute-epoch since rules. It serves CKB holders directly and keeps DAO deposits from being locked longer than needed. Future work, if the committee wants it after DAO v1.1 settles: reminders for Community Fund DAO votes, since DAO deposits are the voting weight.
中文
1. 项目概述
名称：DAO Cycle Alerts
一句话：一个只读的 Telegram 机器人和命令行工具，在每笔 Nervos DAO 存款的 180 个 epoch 周期即将结束时提醒存款人，让他们及时发起取款，避免再等 30 天。
类型：用户工具（Telegram 机器人）+ 开发者工具（npm 包和 CLI）。
2. 团队简介
Yuki Kawata：唯一开发者和维护者。
过往项目：github.com/TheYukiKawata（ton-checkout、arc-tabs、arc-till：基于 TON 和 Arc 的支付工具，部署在 Cloudflare Workers 上）。
联系方式：yuki@yukikawata.fyi（仅限邮件）。
3. 项目背景
Nervos DAO 存款只能在 180 个 epoch（约 30 天）周期结束时解锁（RFC 23）。你可以随时发起取款第一步，但 CKB 会一直锁定到当前周期结束，而且从那一刻起不再获得补偿。
因此，最佳做法是在周期结束前几个小时发起第一步。如果晚了一天，存款会进入新周期，需要再等约 30 天。
目前，想知道存款处于周期的哪个位置，只能打开 Neuron 或其他钱包查看，没有任何工具会提前通知你。Nervos DAO 目前有 16,696 位存款人，存款总额 81.2 亿 CKB（CKB Explorer，2026-09-26）。其中很多人长期持有，并不会每周打开钱包。
场景：Li 在 3 月存入 50,000 CKB，想在 10 月取回用于一笔支出。她在 10 月 3 日打开 Neuron 发起取款，才发现周期已在 10 月 1 日结束，CKB 要到 10 月 31 日才能解锁。
4. 解决方案
用户在 Telegram 发送 /watch <CKB 地址>，机器人列出每笔 DAO 存款及其周期结束时间。
在每个周期结束前 3 天和 12 小时，机器人发送提醒：“50,000 CKB 存款（交易 0xab..）：周期约 12 小时后结束（epoch 9123，约 2026-10-01 14:00 UTC）。请在此之前在钱包中发起取款，届时即可解锁。”
对已处于第一步的存款，当可以执行第二步时，机器人发送：“你的取款中存款现在可以解锁了。”
/list 显示所有监控中的存款；/forget 删除地址和聊天数据。
机器人从不索取私钥、签名或钱包连接，只读取公开链上数据。
与现有工具的区别：钱包只有在打开时才显示倒计时；本工具主动推送提醒，并适用于任何地址，包括冷钱包和多签地址。
5. 技术方案
语言：TypeScript。运行环境：Cloudflare Workers，每 30 分钟执行一次定时任务。存储：Cloudflare D1（聊天 ID、地址、已发送的提醒）。
链上数据：CKB 公共 RPC 和索引器（按 Nervos DAO type script 和用户 lock script 调用 get_cells，用 get_header 获取存款 epoch，用 get_tip_header 获取当前 epoch）。
核心库 dao-cycle（已完成，见第 9 节），基于 CCC：
查找地址上的 Nervos DAO cell，并区分存款 cell（data 为 8 个零字节）和取款中 cell（data 为存款区块高度）；
按 DAO 脚本自身的规则（c/dao.c）计算解锁 epoch：统计从存款到取款经过的 epoch 数，向上取整到 180 的倍数（至少 180），再加到存款 epoch 上。对存款 cell，取款 epoch 取当前 tip，因此结果就是当前周期的结束点；
根据最近 300,000 个区块（约 180 个 epoch）的平均 epoch 时长估算实际时间。
CLI：dao-cycle check <地址> 输出与机器人相同的表格。
难点：epoch 时长会变化，时间估算需要准确。机器人以“约”表述时间，并每 30 分钟重新计算，确保 12 小时提醒使用最新数据。
语言：英文，附中文消息模板。
AI 使用：代码、测试和文档借助 AI 编程代理（Claude）编写。
测试：解锁 epoch 计算有测试覆盖（包括 RFC 23 的示例交易），并已在 150 个主网取款中 cell 上与 CCC 的 calcDaoClaimEpoch 对照。
6. 执行计划
第 1 周：部署在 Cloudflare Workers 上的 Telegram 机器人。/watch、/list、/forget、D1 存储、定时任务。里程碑：机器人在主网上响应 /watch。
第 2 周：提醒功能。3 天和 12 小时提醒、“可以解锁”提醒、提醒去重、中英文消息、simulate 命令。里程碑：提醒上线，dao-cycle 发布到 npm。
第 3 周：种子用户。在 Nervos Talk 和 CKB 社区频道发布。目标：20 个监控地址。收集反馈并修复问题。
第 4 周：结项报告：使用数据、已发送提醒数、用户反馈、资金使用情况。
7. 所需资金与明细
总额：1,000 美元，以 CKB 支付。
技术开发（第 1、2 周）：700 美元。机器人、提醒、simulate 命令、npm 发布、测试、部署。
用户测试（第 3、4 周）：200 美元。种子用户引导、根据反馈修复、结项报告。
托管：100 美元。项目运行在 Cloudflare Workers 免费套餐上；若负载或速率限制需要，用于结项后 12 个月内的付费套餐或专用 RPC。
8. 交付物与验证方式
交付物：
公开 GitHub 仓库（MIT 协议），包含库、CLI 和机器人。
npm 包 dao-cycle（含 CLI）。
主网上线的 Telegram 机器人。
Nervos Talk 上的结项报告。
验证方式（无需审查代码）：
解锁计算：bun install && bun test。预期：全部测试通过，包括 RFC 23 用例（存款于 epoch 2+648/1677，取款中 cell 于 47+382/1605，解锁于 182+648/1677）。
真实数据：bunx dao-cycle check <任意有 DAO 存款的地址>。预期：每笔存款一行，显示下一个周期结束 epoch。可在 Neuron 或 CKB Explorer 中对照同一地址。
机器人：向机器人发送 /watch <地址>。预期：一分钟内返回相同表格。
无需等待 30 天验证提醒时机：bunx dao-cycle simulate <地址> --at-epoch <epoch> 输出机器人在该 epoch 会发送的提醒。
隐私：发送 /forget 后再发送 /list。预期：“没有监控中的地址。”
环境：任意系统上的 Bun 1.x、网络连接、一个 Telegram 账号。总计约 10 分钟。
9. 当前状态与资助范围
当前状态：核心库和 CLI 已可在主网上使用：https://github.com/TheYukiKawata/dao-cycle（MIT 协议）。运行 bun install && bun src/cli.ts check <地址>，即可查看该地址上每个 DAO cell 的解锁 epoch、预计时间和剩余时间。CI 中测试全部通过，包括 RFC 23 示例。解锁计算在主网最新的 150 个取款中 cell 上与 CCC 的 calcDaoClaimEpoch 结果一致。
资助范围：Telegram 机器人、提醒功能、simulate 命令、npm 发布、种子用户和结项报告（第 6、8 节）。
10. CKB 契合度
本工具依赖 CKB 的特性：Nervos DAO type script、以 cell data 区分存款与取款中状态、以及绝对 epoch 的 since 规则。它直接服务 CKB 持有者，避免 DAO 存款被多锁一个周期。后续方向（如委员会在 DAO v1.1 稳定后有需要）：为社区基金 DAO 投票发送提醒，因为 DAO 存款就是投票权重。
recent_posts.content_html:
English

1. Project overview

  • Name: DAO Cycle Alerts
  • One line: A read-only Telegram bot and CLI that tell Nervos DAO depositors when each deposit’s 180-epoch cycle is about to end, so they start a withdrawal in time and do not lose another 30 days.
  • Type: user tool (Telegram bot) plus developer tool (npm package and CLI).

2. Team profile

  • Yuki Kawata: sole developer and maintainer.
  • Past work: TheYukiKawata (Yuki Kawata) · GitHub (ton-checkout, arc-tabs, arc-till: payment tools on TON and Arc, deployed on Cloudflare Workers).
  • Contact: yuki@yukikawata.fyi (email only).

3. Project background

A Nervos DAO deposit unlocks only at the end of a 180-epoch cycle, about 30 days (RFC 23). You can start a withdrawal (phase 1) at any time, but the CKB stays locked until the current cycle ends. The deposit also stops earning compensation from that moment.

So the best time to start phase 1 is a few hours before the cycle ends. If you miss it by a day, the deposit rolls into a new cycle and you wait about 30 more days.

Today you find out where your deposit sits in its cycle only by opening Neuron or another wallet and checking. Nothing tells you ahead of time. There are 16,696 depositors holding 8.12 billion CKB in the DAO (CKB Explorer, 2026-09-26). Many of them hold long term and do not open a wallet every week.

Scenario: Li deposited 50,000 CKB in March and wants the CKB back for a purchase in October. She opens Neuron on October 3, starts the withdrawal, and learns that the cycle ended on October 1. The CKB unlocks on October 31.

4. Solution

  • In Telegram, the user sends /watch <ckb address>. The bot lists each DAO deposit with its cycle end time.
  • The bot sends a message 3 days and 12 hours before each cycle end: “Deposit of 50,000 CKB (tx 0xab..): cycle ends in about 12 hours (epoch 9123, around 2026-10-01 14:00 UTC). Start the withdrawal in your wallet before then to unlock at that time.”
  • For deposits already in phase 1, the bot sends a message when phase 2 becomes possible: “Your withdrawing deposit can be unlocked now.”
  • /list shows every watched deposit. /forget deletes the address and chat data.
  • The bot never asks for keys, signatures or wallet connections. It reads public chain data only.
  • Differences from existing tools: wallets show a countdown only while you have them open. This tool sends the reminder to you, and it works for any address, including cold wallets and multisig.

5. Technical approach

  • Language: TypeScript. Runtime: Cloudflare Workers with a cron trigger every 30 minutes. Storage: Cloudflare D1 (chat id, address, sent reminders).
  • Chain data: CKB public RPC and indexer (get_cells filtered by the Nervos DAO type script and the user’s lock script, get_header for deposit epochs, get_tip_header for the current epoch).
  • Core library dao-cycle (built, see section 9), on top of CCC:
    • find the address’s Nervos DAO cells and classify them as deposited (data is 8 zero bytes) or withdrawing (data is the deposit block number);
    • compute the unlock epoch with the DAO script’s own rule (c/dao.c): count the epochs from deposit to withdrawal, round up to a multiple of 180 (at least 180), add that to the deposit epoch. For a deposited cell the withdrawal epoch is the current tip, so the result is the end of the current cycle;
    • estimate wall-clock time from the average epoch length over the last 300,000 blocks (about 180 epochs).
  • CLI: dao-cycle check <address> prints the same table the bot uses.
  • Hardest part: accurate time estimates, since epoch length changes. The bot states times as “around” and re-checks every 30 minutes, so the 12-hour reminder uses fresh data.
  • Language: English, with Chinese message templates.
  • AI use: code, tests and docs are written with an AI coding agent (Claude).
  • Testing: the unlock epoch math is covered by tests, including RFC 23’s example transaction, and was checked against CCC’s calcDaoClaimEpoch on 150 mainnet withdrawing cells.

6. To-do list

  • Week 1: Telegram bot on Cloudflare Workers. /watch, /list, /forget, D1 storage, cron job. Milestone: bot answers /watch on mainnet.
  • Week 2: Reminders. 3-day and 12-hour messages, “ready to unlock” message, reminder de-duplication, Chinese and English messages, simulate command. Milestone: reminders live, dao-cycle published to npm.
  • Week 3: Seed users. Announce on Nervos Talk and CKB community channels. Target: 20 watched addresses. Collect feedback and fix issues.
  • Week 4: Completion report: usage numbers, reminders sent, feedback, fund usage.

7. Required funding and breakdown

  • Total: $1,000, paid in CKB.
  • Technical work (weeks 1 and 2): $700. Bot, reminders, simulate command, npm release, tests, deployment.
  • User testing (weeks 3 and 4): $200. Onboarding seed users, fixes from feedback, completion report.
  • Hosting: $100. Runs on the Cloudflare Workers free tier. This covers a paid tier or a dedicated RPC endpoint if load or rate limits require it, for 12 months after completion.

8. Deliverables and how to verify

Deliverables:

  1. Public GitHub repository (MIT) with the library, CLI and bot.
  2. npm package dao-cycle with the CLI.
  3. Live Telegram bot on mainnet.
  4. Completion report on Nervos Talk.

How to verify (no code review needed):

  1. Unlock math: bun install && bun test. Expected: all tests pass, including the RFC 23 case (deposit at epoch 2+648/1677, withdrawing cell at 47+382/1605, unlock at 182+648/1677).
  2. CLI against real data: bunx dao-cycle check <any address with a DAO deposit>. Expected: one row per deposit with the next cycle end epoch. Compare it with the same address in Neuron or CKB Explorer.
  3. Bot: send /watch <address> to the bot. Expected: the same table within a minute.
  4. Reminder timing without waiting 30 days: bunx dao-cycle simulate <address> --at-epoch <epoch> prints the reminders the bot would send at that epoch.
  5. Privacy: /forget, then /list. Expected: “No addresses watched.”

Environment: Bun 1.x on any OS, internet access, a Telegram account. About 10 minutes in total.

9. Current state and funded work

  • Current state: the core library and CLI work on mainnet: GitHub - TheYukiKawata/dao-cycle: Find when each Nervos DAO deposit on a CKB address reaches the end of its 180-epoch cycle · GitHub (MIT). Run bun install && bun src/cli.ts check <address> to see each DAO cell on an address with its unlock epoch, estimated time and time left. Tests pass in CI, including the RFC 23 example. The unlock math gave the same result as CCC’s calcDaoClaimEpoch on the 150 newest withdrawing cells on mainnet.
  • Funded work: the Telegram bot, reminders, simulate command, npm release, seed users and the completion report (sections 6 and 8).

10. CKB alignment

The tool depends on CKB features: the Nervos DAO type script, cell data as the deposit/withdrawing marker, and absolute-epoch since rules. It serves CKB holders directly and keeps DAO deposits from being locked longer than needed. Future work, if the committee wants it after DAO v1.1 settles: reminders for Community Fund DAO votes, since DAO deposits are the voting weight.

recent_posts.content_text:

topics.title: CellScript 0.30: Abstractions, Bytes, and the Cost

recent_posts.topic_title: CellScript 0.30: Abstractions, Bytes, and the Cost
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
A follow-up on the immediate encoding mentioned in section 5. I gave it one sentence and a byte count there, which skipped over what the compiler was actually doing. The work on 0.31 makes that worth revisiting.
The original post recorded a 464-byte saving from shorter constant loads. That came from a fairly simple improvement developed on 0.26b and carried into 0.30: stop using two instructions when one will do.
For anyone who doesn’t usually read assembly, an immediate is a number written directly into an instruction. “Add 5 to this register” carries the 5 in the instruction itself. A register is one of the small storage locations the machine uses while calculating.
There is only so much room for the number. RISC-V’s ADDI instruction has a signed 12-bit field, enough for −2048 through 2047. Larger values need another encoding or several steps to construct them.
Assembly makes this look simpler than it is. You can write:
li a0, 5
That asks the assembler to put 5 in register a0. But li is shorthand; the assembler still has to choose the real instructions. In CellScript 0.25, this used the general two-instruction form:
lui a0, 0 # prepare the upper part
addi a0, a0, 5 # add the lower part
By 0.30, the assembler could emit just:
addi a0, zero, 5
The zero register always reads as zero, so that gives us 5 directly. Each removed instruction saves four bytes. The historical relation sample had 116 such opportunities, accounting for those 464 bytes. The much larger 3,968-byte saving in the same section came from removing file padding; that was a separate change. The earlier implementation notes have the breakdown.
Large constants still had a rather expensive fallback. The assembler built them one byte at a time: start with the first byte, shift left by eight bits, add the next byte, and repeat. That produced 15 instructions for a 64-bit value, even when many of those steps were adding zero.
2^56 is a useful example. Written in decimal, it looks large: 72057594037927936. In binary, it is just a 1 followed by 56 zeros. There is no reason to assemble all eight bytes separately when we can do this:
addi a0, zero, 1
slli a0, a0, 56
Put 1 in the register, then shift it left 56 places. The result is identical, but preparing it takes two instructions and eight bytes instead of 15 instructions and 60 bytes.
That is the next step implemented on 0.31. The new planner splits constants into pieces that fit the instructions and combines shifts where it can. It checks that the chosen sequence reconstructs the exact value and compares it with the old sequence, which remains available as a fallback. Arbitrary constants won’t all reduce to two instructions, but simple bit patterns no longer have to pay for the byte-by-byte construction. The planner itself is fairly small.
I wanted to separate that benefit from the other work on 0.31, so the follow-up measurements include a control with only the new immediate planner enabled against the reproduced 0.30 backend:
Policy fixture
ELF bytes, before → after
Worst successful transaction cycles, before → after
8 actions, 32-byte argument
11,680 → 10,000
14,158 → 13,678
64 actions, 32-byte argument
73,440 → 61,008
29,822 → 26,654
In the 64-action fixture, that is about 16.9% fewer bytes and 10.6% fewer cycles from immediate encoding alone. These are specific measured workloads; the result depends on which constants occur and how often the code using them executes.

topics.title: Paying a .cell name over Fiber on testnet: what it took

recent_posts.topic_title: Paying a .cell name over Fiber on testnet: what it took
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
fiber-card3200×1800 251 KB
In early September we checked whether a .cell name can work as a Fiber payment endpoint: a payer reads the name, finds the node, and pays it without asking the payee for anything. On testnet it did, including a payment routed through a public hub. Two things had to be fixed on the payee’s side first, and they are the useful part of this post.
The records
A name publishes two records:
fiber.node: the node’s public key, 33 raw bytes. Fiber’s RPC takes it as bare hex in target_pubkey, so strip any 0x prefix at that boundary.
fiber.addr: a multiaddr, as text.
There is no invoice record. An invoice is made for one payment, so the payer keysends to the published key, or asks for an invoice out of band. A wrong or stale key is a denial of payment, not a theft: payments settle against the node key, so publishing someone else’s key sends the money to them.
The records for telmo.cell went on chain in 0xba70f36da3101ef7439fbc417351f714ca04bcc629d37d481808764446a713a1, Pudge block 22301240, 2026-09-03 22:27 UTC. Like every record, they sit in the witness and the cell commits to their hash.
What we measured
In every step the payee was addressed only by the key read back from the name.
Step
Result
Dial
A node with no bootnodes dialled the published multiaddr and completed the handshake in about 3 s. The payee logged the inbound peer from a public IP.
Direct keysend, 1.23 CKB
Success, fee 0, no invoice. Payee +123,000,000 shannons, payer -123,000,000.
Routed keysend, 2.34 CKB
To a node the payer had no channel with: Success, fee 234,000 shannons (0.1%).
Pay by name, 4.56 CKB
An independent node, with its own identity and network, one channel to a public hub and no channel to the payee, resolved telmo.cell and paid it: Success, fee 456,000 shannons (0.1%), payee +456,000,000 exactly.
The fee is how we know the payments were forwarded. A direct channel costs 0, and each routed payment cost exactly the hub’s advertised tlc_fee_proportional_millionths, 1000.
The payments themselves are off chain. The evidence is each node’s payment status and channel balances, which we logged. The only on-chain part is the records’ transaction above.
What had to be true first
A private channel makes the node invisible. The payee’s only channel was private, so it did not appear in graph_nodes and no other node could compute a route to it. The name resolved perfectly to a node the network could not see.
A new channel is outbound only. A public 2000 CKB channel to a hub still could not receive, because the other side held nothing pointing back. The payee had to spend 200 CKB out through it first. After that it held an announced 1901 CKB channel with about 200 CKB of inbound liquidity, which was the most a single routed payment into the name could carry.
So being payable is something the node operator arranges, not something a name declares.
Limits
This was testnet, between 3 and 4 September. The namespace it ran on was replaced by a new deployment on 4 September, and the payee node is no longer running, so the exact setup cannot be re-run. The record format is unchanged.
Today no name publishes a Fiber node: 0 of 62 on mainnet and 0 of 43 on testnet, checked on 2026-09-27.
Paying over Fiber needs a running fnn node. We know of no end-user wallet that pays Fiber today, so this is for node operators and services, not for a person with a phone.
Trying it
A name’s records come back from GET https://cellula.id/api/resolve/<name> (or testnet.cellula.id) with a fiber field, null when the name publishes none. From there it is a send_payment on your own node, with target_pubkey set to the key without 0x, and keysend: true.
If you run a Fiber node and want to try paying a name, or see a better endpoint to publish than a key and a multiaddr, say so here.
